description:
We are a multidisciplinary team of five passionate Computer Science and technology enthusiasts participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Our team combines skills in Frontend Development, Python Backend Development, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, 3D Graphics, and Networking & Cybersecurity.

We believe in combining creativity, collaboration, and technical innovation to solve real-world challenges. For this challenge, we are developing Lunar Landing Site Navigator.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive platform designed to support safer and more informed lunar landing site selection, particularly in the Moon’s south polar region.

The platform combines NASA lunar elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with solar and Earth position data from NASA JPL Horizons to analyze real terrain horizons, sunlight availability, and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities. Users can explore candidate landing sites, visualize terrain, examine environmental conditions over selected date ranges, and compare up to three locations side by side.

By evaluating how surrounding terrain affects solar exposure and Earth visibility, the platform helps identify potential operational challenges that could impact power generation and communication during lunar missions.

Our goal is to transform complex lunar datasets into clear, interactive, and mission-relevant insights, supporting better-informed decisions for future robotic and human exploration of the Moon.
details:
Project Overview

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive platform designed to help mission planners identify and compare potential lunar landing locations, particularly in the Moon’s south polar region.

The Problem

The Moon’s south pole presents unique challenges for future missions. The Sun remains close to the horizon, while surrounding mountains and craters can obstruct sunlight and direct communication with Earth. These conditions can cause power interruptions and communication blackouts, making landing site selection and mission scheduling difficult.

NASA Data Sources

Our project uses multiple NASA data sources:

  • NASA/JPL Horizons API: Provides the Sun’s and Earth’s positions as observed from selected lunar locations, including azimuth and elevation.
  • NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA: Provides lunar elevation data used to analyze real surface topography and calculate terrain horizons.
  • NASA PGDA: Provides access to the LOLA elevation datasets.
  • Artemis III Candidate Landing Regions: Used as candidate locations for analysis and comparison.
  • Apollo Landing Site Data (NSSDC): Provides historical landing locations for additional comparisons.

How It Works

The platform combines celestial positioning with real lunar terrain analysis.

First, NASA JPL Horizons provides the positions of the Sun and Earth over a selected date range. Second, NASA LOLA elevation maps are processed to calculate the surrounding terrain horizon in 360 directions, up to 250 km, while accounting for lunar curvature.

The system then compares the Sun’s and Earth’s elevations with the terrain horizon at each time step. Earth visibility also includes a 2-degree antenna elevation margin.

This allows the application to calculate sunlight availability, Earth communication windows, simultaneous visibility, and the longest periods of darkness.

Technology Stack

Backend and Scientific Computing: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, and Requests.

Frontend and Visualization: React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei.

Development and Collaboration: Visual Studio Code, Git, and GitHub.

Benefits and Innovation

Users can explore candidate landing sites, select mission date ranges, compare up to three locations, and visualize results through interactive timelines, terrain horizon panoramas, and 3D sky views.

Our key innovation is evaluating solar and Earth visibility against the actual surrounding lunar terrain rather than relying on a simplified flat-horizon model.

The platform aims to make complex lunar environmental data easier to understand and use, helping mission planners assess operational risks, compare landing opportunities, and make better-informed decisions for future lunar exploration.
